title: Language Exchange Café: Meeting New People
summary: At a café language exchange, you trade languages with new people: you read their stickers, shake hands, say your first name, keep the talk going with follow-up questions and your own stories, and end in a kind way.

blocks.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Today we spend an evening at a language exchange in a café. We learn how the evening works, how to order and how to introduce ourselves. Then we practise long conversations and a kind goodbye.

items.prompt: Do you like meeting new people? Why or why not?
What do you usually say first when you meet someone new?
Which language would you like to practise with a native speaker?

blocks.title: Part 1: How a Language Exchange Works
paragraphs: **A language exchange is a trade: you give something, and you get something back.** You help someone with your language, and they help you with theirs. For example, you speak Japanese and want to practise English. So you look for an English speaker who wants to practise Japanese.
**Everyone is a teacher and a student at the same time.** When you help with your language, you are the teacher. When the other person helps you, you are the student.
**In this lesson, you visit the Dutch Language Café in The Hague.** The Hague is a city in the Netherlands. The café has a language exchange every Thursday evening.

**Every visitor gets a language sticker and wears it on their shirt.** Write your languages on two lines, so people can see the difference. Your native language is the first language you learned as a child. It goes on the Speak line. For example:
- Speak: Japanese
- Practise: English

**A sticker shows you who can help you.** The room is full of strangers, people you do not know. But with one look at a sticker, you know their languages. It also gives you your first question. Do you see Spanish on the Practise line? Ask: I see you study Spanish. Why?

**The evening has a clear plan:**
- 19:30: arrive and get your sticker.
- 20:00: speed exchange, 3 minutes with each person.
- 20:30: language tables, with one language at each table.
- 21:10: change tables if you want.

**In the speed exchange, you take turns choosing the language.** First one of you chooses, then the other, so both people practise. After 3 minutes, you move to the next person. Why so short? In a short time, you meet many new people.

blocks.title: Check: Part 1: How a Language Exchange Works

items.prompt: Why does every visitor wear a language sticker?
items.answer: So other people see their languages and know who can help them.

rows.example: My native language is Spanish, and I want to practise Dutch.
I see you study English. Why? – For my job.

rows.meaning: when the person has no sticker
rows.example: Which languages do you speak? – Dutch and a little Japanese.

blocks.title: Part 2: Ordering at the Café
paragraphs: **Your €11 ticket includes the snacks and the games.** Included means they are in the price. The snacks are popcorn, crisps and nuts. You eat them at your table.
**Drinks are not included, so you buy them at the bar.** You order from the bartender, the person who works behind the bar. You buy food there too.

**On the menu, you see a funny name: koffie verkeerd.** In English, it means wrong coffee. Why wrong? A normal Dutch coffee has only a little milk. Koffie verkeerd has a lot of warm milk, often more than the coffee. So it is the wrong way around.
**If you are hungry, try an empanada.** It is small and baked, with food inside. At this café, you choose cheese, meat or spinach.

**When you do not understand, do not just say yes.** A bar is loud, and a menu has new words. Ask: Sorry, can you say that again? Or ask about one word: What does spinach mean? At a language café, everyone is a student, so questions are normal.

blocks.title: Check: Part 2: Ordering at the Café

items.prompt: What does koffie verkeerd mean, and why?
items.answer: Wrong coffee, because it has much more milk than a normal Dutch coffee.

rows.meaning: to ask what a price pays for (for more than one thing, say Are ... included?)
rows.example: Is breakfast included? – Yes, it is.
Can I have a koffie verkeerd, please? – Sure, that's €4.00.

rows.meaning: when you hear a new word
rows.example: What does verkeerd mean? – It means wrong.

rows.term: Sorry, can you say that again?
rows.meaning: when you did not hear or understand
rows.example: That's ten fifty. – Sorry, can you say that again? – Ten euros fifty.

blocks.title: Part 3: Introducing Yourself
paragraphs: **In the Netherlands, people shake hands with someone new and say their name.** Often it is only the first name: Hi! I'm Sanne. In Japan, many people bow, or bend forward, and say their family name.
**A hello without your name is rude, or not polite.** Why? Your name tells people who you are. It also tells them what to call you all evening. So when you hear a new name, say your name too.

**At a first meeting, do not ask: How are you?** For many Dutch people, it is a real question, not just a hello. They ask it when they really want to know the answer. So they usually ask people they already know.
**Save How are you? for next Thursday, when you meet again.** At a first meeting, just say hello and your name.
**A speed exchange is short.** So say three things: your name, your city and why you study the language. Daan says: Hi! I'm Daan. I live in The Hague. I study Japanese because I'm going to Tokyo.
**The reason is the most useful part.** It gives the other person a question. For example: What do you want to see in Tokyo? When you finish, ask back: What about you?

items.prompt: Why do Dutch people not ask How are you? at a first meeting?
items.answer: For them it is a real question, so they ask people they already know.

rows.example: What do you do? – I'm an engineer. – Oh, I'm a teacher.

rows.meaning: to say why you learn a language
rows.example: Why do you study Dutch? – I study Dutch because I work in The Hague.

rows.meaning: to ask the same question back
rows.example: I'm a teacher. What about you? – I work at a hotel.

blocks.title: Part 4: Keeping the Conversation Going
paragraphs: **The best tool for a long conversation is the follow-up question.** A follow-up question is a question about what the other person just said. It stays with their idea. A new question jumps to a new idea, for example: Do you like football?

**Each answer gives you the next follow-up question:**
- Lucía: I moved here from Valencia.
- You: Really? Why did you move here?
- Lucía: For work. I work at a hotel.
- You: What do you do at the hotel?

**In 2017, scientists at Harvard University studied conversations between strangers.** People who asked more questions were liked more by their partners. Follow-up questions worked best. Why? A follow-up question shows that you are really listening.

**But a good conversation goes both ways.** If you never talk about yourself, people may think you are hiding something. So react to what you hear: Really? Me too! or That sounds fun! Then tell something about yourself, and ask back.

blocks.title: Check: Part 4: Keeping the Conversation Going

items.answer: A question about what the other person just said.

rows.meaning: to ask for the reason after someone tells you something
rows.example: I started Dutch last year. – Why did you start? – For my job.

rows.term: How long have you lived here?
rows.meaning: to ask about time in a place
rows.example: How long have you lived here? – About five years.

rows.meaning: when the same is true for you
rows.example: I love koffie verkeerd. – Really? Me too!

rows.meaning: when someone tells you a nice plan or hobby
rows.example: I'm going to the beach this weekend. – That sounds fun!

blocks.title: Part 5: Ending Well
paragraphs: **At 21:30, the exchange ends. Do not just walk away.** The other person gave you their time. So thank them with kind words: It was nice to talk to you.

**Do you want to keep in touch? Ask for WhatsApp.** Keep in touch means you talk or write again later. In the Netherlands, WhatsApp is by far the most used app for messages. So almost everyone you meet can say yes.
**The exchange is every Thursday, so say goodbye for one week:** See you next Thursday! Next time, you can ask: How are you?

items.prompt: Why is it easy to keep in touch on WhatsApp in the Netherlands?
items.answer: It is by far the most used app for messages there, so almost everyone has it.

rows.term: It was nice to talk to you
rows.meaning: when you leave a new person
rows.example: I have to go now. It was nice to talk to you! – You too. Bye!

rows.term: Can I add you on WhatsApp?
rows.example: Can I add you on WhatsApp? – Sure! Here's my number.

blocks.title: Scene: Arriving and Ordering
paragraphs: It is Thursday, 19:30. You walk into the Dutch Language Café, Herengracht 13A, The Hague. A host is at the door, and a bartender works at the bar.
Phrases to use: My native language is ... / Is ... included? / Can I have ...? / What does ... mean?
Your goal: get your sticker, then order a drink and food at the bar.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Hi, I'm here for the language exchange.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Welcome! What's your name?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I'm (your name). I signed up online.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Yes, here you are on my list. Is this your first time here?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Yes, it is.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Great, welcome! Where are you from?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I'm from (your city), in Japan.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Oh, nice! Here's your sticker. Please write the languages you speak and the languages you want to practise.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: OK. My native language is Japanese, and I want to practise English.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Perfect. The speed exchange starts at 20:00.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Thank you. Is the popcorn included?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Yes, the popcorn, crisps and nuts are in your ticket, and the games too. Drinks are not included. You buy them at the bar.

turns.speaker: Bartender
turns.text: Hi! What would you like?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Can I have a koffie verkeerd, please?

turns.speaker: Bartender
turns.text: Sure. Anything to eat?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: What is an empanada?

turns.speaker: Bartender
turns.text: It's small and baked, with food inside. We have cheese, meat or spinach.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Sorry, what does spinach mean?

turns.speaker: Bartender
turns.text: It's a green vegetable with soft leaves.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Ah, OK. A cheese one, please. How much is it?

turns.speaker: Bartender
turns.text: The koffie verkeerd is €4.00, and the empanada is €6.50. That's €10.50, please.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Here you go. Which languages do you speak?

turns.speaker: Bartender
turns.text: Dutch, English and some German. Enjoy the exchange!

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Thank you! Have a nice evening.

blocks.title: Scene: Meeting Your Table
paragraphs: At 19:45, you sit down with your coffee and empanada. A Dutch woman sits next to you. Her sticker says she speaks Dutch and English. She practises Spanish.
Phrases to use: I see you study ... / I study ... because ... / What about you? / That sounds fun!
Your goal: shake hands, say your name and get to know her.

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: Hi! I'm Sanne.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Hi, Sanne! I'm (your name). Nice to meet you.

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: Nice to meet you too. I see Japanese on your sticker. Where are you from?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I'm from (your city), in Japan. What about you?

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: I'm from here, The Hague. I come to this café every Thursday.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Every Thursday? Wow! I see you study Spanish. Why?

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: I go to Spain every summer. I want to order food and talk to people in Spanish, not English!

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: That sounds fun! Is Spanish hard?

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: Some parts, yes. The verbs are hard for me! And you? Why do you study English?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I study English because (your reason for learning English).

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: That's a great reason. What do you do?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I'm a/an (your job). What about you?

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: I'm a teacher. I teach children at a primary school.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Really? Do you like it?

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: Yes, I love it. But on the weekend, I want a quiet day! What do you do in your free time?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: In my free time, I like (your hobby).

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: Oh, nice! I play ping pong. There's a table here at the café. Do you play?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: A little. But I'm not very good!

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: Me neither! Let's play later.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: It's 20:00, everyone! The speed exchange starts now. Please find a partner.

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: Oh, it's time! Good luck!

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Thanks, Sanne. See you later!

blocks.title: Scene: The Speed Exchange
paragraphs: At 20:00, the speed exchange starts: 3 minutes with each person. Your first partner's sticker says he speaks Dutch and English and practises Japanese.
Phrases to use: I'm a ... / I'm an ... / Sorry, can you say that again? / That sounds fun!
Your goal: speak English, then teach Daan a Japanese phrase for his trip.

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Hi! I'm Daan.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Hi, Daan! I'm (your name). Nice to meet you.

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Nice to meet you too. We take turns choosing the language. You can choose first.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: English, please. I see Japanese on your sticker!

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Yes, I study Japanese. I started six months ago, so I know only a little. What do you do?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I'm a/an (your job). What about you?

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: I'm an engineer. I make machines for factories.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Sorry, can you say that again? It's very loud in here.

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: I'm an engineer. I make machines.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Oh, cool! Why do you study Japanese?

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: I'm going to Tokyo in April, for two weeks!

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: That sounds fun! What do you want to do there?

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Eat a lot of ramen and see old temples. And you? Why do you study English?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I study English because (your reason for learning English).

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Good reason! OK, now it's my turn. Japanese, please. What can I say in a shop in Tokyo?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Say kore o hitotsu kudasai. It means this one, please.

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Kore o... sorry, can you say that again?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Kore o hitotsu kudasai. Kore is this, hitotsu is one, and kudasai is please give me.

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Kore o hitotsu kudasai! Is that right?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Yes, perfect! Point at the thing you want and say it.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Time's up! Please move to the next person.

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Thank you! That's really useful.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: It was nice to talk to you, Daan. Have a great trip!

blocks.title: Scene: The English Table
paragraphs: At 20:30, you sit at the English table with Sanne. A new woman sits down. Her sticker says she speaks Spanish and English. She practises Dutch.
Phrases to use: Why did you ...? / How long have you lived here? / Really? Me too! / Can I add you on WhatsApp?
Your goal: ask follow-up questions, talk about yourself and keep in touch.

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: Hi! I'm Lucía.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Hi, Lucía! I'm (your name). Nice to meet you. Where are you from?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: Nice to meet you too. I'm from Valencia, in Spain, but I moved to The Hague.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Really? Why did you move here?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: For work. I work at a big hotel.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Oh, nice! What do you do at the hotel?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: I work at the front desk. I say hello to the guests and give them their room keys.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: How long have you lived here?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: Two years. I study Dutch, but it's hard! And I miss the sun in Valencia.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: What is Valencia like?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: It's warm and sunny, and the food is great. What about you? What do you do?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I'm a/an (your job). In my free time, I like (your hobby).

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: Oh, nice! I see you study English. Why?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I study English because (your reason for learning English).

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: That's a great reason. Oh, you have a koffie verkeerd! I really love coffee.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Really? Me too! I drink coffee every morning. But this is my first koffie verkeerd, and it's very good.

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: I have one here every Thursday. Next week, try the empanadas too!

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I had a cheese one tonight. It was great!

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: It's 21:30, everyone. The exchange is over. Thank you for coming!

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: It was nice to talk to you, Lucía. Can I add you on WhatsApp?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: Sure! Here's my number. Let's practise again soon.

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: Are you coming next Thursday?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Yes! See you next Thursday!

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: See you next Thursday! Bye!

blocks.title: Speaking
paragraphs: With a partner, practise the scenes in time order, then change roles.

blocks.title: Final Reflection
blocks.intro: Follow-up questions and your own stories keep a language exchange going.

items.prompt: Would you like to go to a language exchange? Why or why not?
Someone says, I just started a new job. What follow-up question can you ask?
What three things will you say when you introduce yourself?
